title: One more throw
hookLine: Duryodhana offers the earth; Yudhishthira refuses, then stakes everything again
carry: samskara: old habits cut deep grooves
tomorrow: two cousins, two maces. who taught them both?

cards: An offer rises from under the water. Take the whole earth, Duryodhana says, in effect. My friends are dead, my brothers are dead.
I have no wish to rule an empty kingdom. I'll go to the forest, dressed in deerskins, and live there. It sounds like surrender, the end of the war handed over without another blow.
And Yudhishthira, standing on the bank, refuses.

teach.b: It isn't yours to give, Yudhishthira answers, in Ganguli's telling. Before the war you wouldn't give us as much land as the point of a needle would cover. Now that you've lost it, you offer it all as a gift?
A warrior doesn't take a kingdom as charity. Come out and fight. Then he goes further.
Choose any one of us, he says, with any weapon you like. Beat that one, and the kingdom is yours. Krishna is alarmed.
You've staked everything again on a single throw, he says in effect; none of you but Bhima can face Duryodhana with the mace, and even Bhima has less skill.
Some readers hear the old dice game here: the king who lost everything once by gambling has just gambled again.
Hindu thought has a word for that pull: samskara. Every act leaves an impression in the mind, and impressions repeated become grooves, so the next act slides the same way.
Yudhishthira is the dharma king, wise and truthful, and the groove of the dice is still in him.
It's one reason Hindu practice leans on the daily: a morning prayer, a name repeated on the mala, a lamp lit at dusk. No single day is magic. Repeated good acts cut new grooves.
Duryodhana rises out of the lake, dripping, mace on his shoulder, and he chooses the mace. And Bhima steps forward to meet him.

how: The exchange at the lake, from the Shalya Parva, is retold in readings and serials of the Mahabharata, and Duryodhana's earlier refusal of even a needle's point of land is recalled there.

s: Yudhishthira accepted the kingdom Duryodhana offered from the lake
he refused it: it wasn't Duryodhana's to give, and a warrior doesn't take a kingdom as charity.
Krishna was alarmed because Yudhishthira staked everything on one fight
some readers hear the old dice game: the gambler gambled again.
in Hindu thought, a samskara vanishes the moment you decide to change
impressions repeated become grooves; it takes repeated practice to cut new ones.

games.q: you've sworn off scrolling at 1am three times this month, and here you are again. by today's teaching, what fits?
o: a small daily practice, repeated, to cut a new groove.
one big dramatic vow, then hope.
accept it; that's just who you are.
games.why: samskaras are grooves cut by repetition. Hindus answer with daily practice, japa, prayer, a lamp at dusk, because repeated acts cut new grooves.

practice: Japa is an old Hindu practice: one name or mantra, repeated, often on a mala of a hundred and eight beads. Sit easy, hands open.
If you pray, repeat a name of God you love, quietly, for the rest of the sit: Ram, Krishna, Om, whichever is yours. If you don't pray, repeat one short word you want more of, like peace.
Each time the mind slides off, bring it back. That's a new groove being cut.

wordCard.voice: Shalya. An offer refused at the lake's edge, a gamble made, and a king rising from the water to fight.

orig.note: mace: the weapon Duryodhana chooses when he rises from the lake.
